scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Scenario:
AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced and emotionally charged situation, and while I can’t assign a strict "right" or "wrong" binary (since relationships involve complex dynamics), I’ll break it down objectively to help you reflect on what might have gone wrong—and how to address it. **Your answer would likely be <1> (AITA), but with important context to consider.** --- ### **Why This Might Not Be Just "Constructive Criticism"** 1. **Timing and Delivery Matter** - You framed this as "helpful," but the way it escalated suggests your girlfriend felt **humiliated or unsupported** rather than coached. Even if your intentions were good, the **method** (especially in front of your mom) likely felt like criticism disguised as kindness. - **Example:** Saying, *"My mom could teach you how to cook"* in front of her isn’t just offering a suggestion—it implies her skills are lacking, which can feel like a **public shaming**. Your girlfriend might have interpreted it as: *"Your cooking is bad, but my mom can fix it."* 2. **The "Strike" Isn’t About the Food—It’s About Control and Respect** - Her reaction isn’t just about cooking; it’s about **feeling valued and respected**. If she’s been cooking for you for months and suddenly feels judged (even indirectly), it can trigger insecurity, especially if she’s already self-conscious about her skills. - **Red flag:** She’s not just avoiding cooking—she’s **refusing to cook for you at all**, which is a bigger deal than a temporary cooking strike. This suggests the issue runs deeper than technique. 3. **Power Dynamics in the Relationship** - You moved in together after 2 years of dating, and you’ve taken on the role of the "better cook" while she handles the timing. This can create an **imbalance of effort** (even if unintentional). If she feels like she’s carrying the cooking load while also dealing with criticism, it’s a recipe for resentment. - **Question to ask yourself:** *Have I ever acknowledged how much effort she puts into cooking for us?* Even if her food isn’t gourmet, it’s still a **daily act of care**—and unsolicited critiques can make that feel unappreciated. 4. **The "Apology" Isn’t Enough (Yet)** - You apologized for the **specific incident** (mentioning your mom), but her broader reaction suggests she needs **more than an apology**—she needs to feel **heard and validated**. Saying *"I’m sorry I made you feel bad"* without addressing the underlying issue (e.g., *"I realize I could’ve handled this differently and I’ll work on being more supportive"*) won’t fully resolve it. --- ### **What You Could Do Now** 1. **Acknowledge Her Feelings First** - Instead of defending your actions, **validate her emotions**. Try: > *"I get why you’d feel hurt. I never meant to make you feel bad about cooking for us—I just wanted to help. I realize now that I could’ve handled it differently, and I’m sorry if it made you feel exposed."* - This shifts the focus from *"You’re overreacting"* to *"I see how this affected you."* 2. **Take Responsibility for the Bigger Picture** - Admit that the criticism (even well-intentioned) contributed to her withdrawal. Say something like: > *"I realize now that my comments about cooking—even when I thought I was being helpful—made you feel like I didn’t appreciate what you were doing for us. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry."* 3. **Propose a Fresh Start** - Offer to **cook together** or take turns in a way that feels collaborative, not competitive. For example: > *"Let’s figure out a way to make cooking feel like a team effort again. Maybe we can try a new recipe together or take a cooking class—no pressure, just fun."* - This shows you’re **invested in fixing the dynamic**, not just the food. 4. **Address the Power Imbalance** - If she’s been cooking for you for months, **acknowledge the effort** and suggest a compromise, like: > *"I know you’ve been doing most of the cooking, and I appreciate it. Maybe we can alternate nights or split tasks so it feels fairer?"* 5. **Give Her Space to Rebuild Trust** - If she’s still refusing to cook, don’t push. Instead, **show through actions** that you respect her. Maybe: - Help with other chores (cleaning, laundry) to lighten her load. - Compliment her cooking **genuinely** (e.g., *"This tastes great, and I love that you made it!"*). - If she’s open to it, suggest a **low-pressure cooking experiment** (e.g., making a simple dish side by side). --- ### **Why She Might Not Be "Crazy"** - **Rejection sensitivity:** Some people (especially women) are more sensitive to perceived criticism, especially in areas tied to self-worth (like cooking). - **Fear of failure:** If she’s already insecure about her skills, unsolicited advice—even from a partner—can feel like a **personal attack**. - **Control vs. support:** She might feel like she’s being **controlled** (e.g., *"You’re not good enough, but my mom is"*) rather than **supported**. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not *wrong* for wanting to help, but **how you help matters**. The goal in relationships isn’t to be "right"—it’s to **make your partner feel secure, respected, and valued**. Right now, your girlfriend needs to feel **seen in her effort**, not judged in her skill. Would you like help drafting a specific apology or conversation starter? Or would you prefer to explore how to rebuild trust in other areas of the relationship?
